title: Thinking About Homeschooling This Fall? Don't Just Leave School -- Plan the Transition
author: Keller, Shari
summary: The decision to homeschool is only the beginning; the harder work is designing the transition intentionally rather than defaulting to replicating school at home. Families benefit from first identifying with specificity what was not working -- the pacing, the social environment, the slow erosion of curiosity -- before planning what to build next, because without that diagnosis they tend to recreate the same friction in a different setting. The transition also belongs to the child, not only the parent: children have genuine attachments to rhythms, relationships, and routines that should be acknowledged and explored rather than assumed. The deschooling period -- the early weeks when nothing looks like learning -- is not a gap to be filled but a necessary settling; children who have spent years in externally paced structures need time to recover their own initiative before organic learning re-emerges. Summer functions as a bridge, not a pause, best used for light social connection and unhurried observation rather than curriculum shopping or schedule building. The parent's role shifts from instructor to co-learner: moving alongside the child, following curiosity, and gradually recognizing that learning is happening even when it does not look like school.
points: * Before planning homeschool, identify with specificity what was not working in school -- the actual felt friction, not the version that sounds reasonable when said aloud -- to avoid recreating the same problems at home. * The transition belongs to the child too: acknowledging what they will miss, what they are glad to leave, and what social connections they need reframes the shift as something done together rather than done to them. * The deschooling period looks like nothing -- sleeping later, drifting, moving slowly -- but is a necessary recovery period during which a child's intrinsic initiative begins to re-emerge after years of external pacing. * Friendships are not tied to a school building; they are tied to time, proximity, and shared experience, and can reorganize around homeschool community if families make small, consistent efforts during the summer transition. * Progress markers shift from grades and benchmarks to whether a child sticks with something when it is hard, asks questions that lead somewhere, and begins taking ownership of their time in small but meaningful ways.
quotes: Leaving school isn't just removing something from your child's life -- it's stepping out of a structure that has been organizing their days for years.
That's where people often end up recreating the same experience at home -- just in a different setting.

What's happening here isn't a problem. It's a shift. For a long time, your child has been moving inside a system that sets the pace, defines the work, and constantly measures how it's going. When that system falls away, nothing immediately replaces it.
You begin to move alongside your child instead of ahead of them -- looking things up together, figuring things out in real time, paying attention to where their interest is pulling them.
